paragraphs: Comparing methods for rendering human bodies with neural radiance fields becomes difficult when each method uses different datasets, evaluation settings, or measurements. This paper tackles that comparison problem by developing a shared benchmark. Its purpose is to make differences between methods easier to interpret through a more consistent evaluation process.

The researchers study unified evaluation settings and metrics, then test existing models on varied, challenging scenes. They also construct a benchmark for generalization across people, using pretraining on large datasets. This adds an evaluation question beyond rendering a particular person: how effectively can a method carry what it has learned to other subjects?

The work also examines components relevant to animating people and generalizing across subjects. Using this analysis, the researchers adapt HumanNeRF, a method using monocular videos, into a generalizable baseline. The contribution therefore combines evaluation infrastructure with a concrete reference method. It gives subsequent work a shared basis for studying rendering, animation, and transfer across people.
neurips-2023-a-comprehensive-benchmark-f.tldr: The paper establishes shared human NeRF benchmarks and a generalizable HumanNeRF baseline to support fairer comparisons.

paragraphs: Fitting a linear model to an extremely large dataset can make ordinary least squares impractical under limited computing resources. One response is sketching: compress the data and fit the model using that smaller representation. This paper investigates the accuracy limits of such approaches when the number of variables can grow with the number of observations.

The authors derive detailed lower bounds on conditional mean squared error. For methods that select observations through sampling, these bounds identify an attainable optimal convergence rate. Their analysis indicates that, in high dimensions, sampling strategies have little scope to improve the convergence rate over uniform sampling. This motivates changing how the compressed observations are constructed.

The proposed method forms a small collection of averaged observations that still obey the linear model, then estimates coefficients from those averages. The asymptotic analysis shows that this approach can converge faster than the optimal rate for sampling methods. Theoretical and numerical findings support its combination of statistical accuracy and low computational cost.
neurips-2023-a-fast-and-accurate-estimat.tldr: Averaging observations provides a compact linear regression estimator that can converge faster than methods based on sampling observations.

paragraphs: When choices have several objectives, there may be no single best option. The Pareto set captures options whose trade-offs cannot be improved across the objectives simultaneously. This paper studies how to identify such options with a specified confidence level when information must be gathered by repeatedly sampling different choices.

Finding the exact Pareto set can require many samples. One existing relaxation permits the answer to include additional options that are nearly optimal. The authors also examine relaxations that seek a relevant subset of the Pareto set. They introduce Adaptive Pareto Exploration, a single sampling strategy that works with different stopping rules to accommodate these different targets.

The analysis quantifies the sample requirements of the resulting combinations, including the savings possible when identifying at most k Pareto-optimal options. A practical demonstration adaptively explores Covid-19 vaccination strategies using multiple immunogenicity criteria. The reported performance supports the usefulness of matching the identification target to the desired collection of trade-offs, rather than always requiring the complete exact set.
neurips-2023-adaptive-algorithms-for-rel.tldr: Adaptive Pareto Exploration uses one sampling strategy with different stopping rules to efficiently identify relaxed Pareto sets.

paragraphs: Text-guided generative models can combine concepts that differ substantially from one another. This paper asks what structure inside a model could support that ability. It focuses on score-based models and investigates the idea that concepts occupy distinct subspaces within an internal representation, making their contributions accessible to mathematical manipulation.

The authors formalize what it means for a concept to be represented by a subspace. They identify a natural representation in which to study this structure and develop a simple procedure for locating the portion associated with a chosen concept. This turns the broad intuition of disentangled concepts into a concrete way to identify and work with parts of a representation.

Once a concept-associated component is identified, algebraic operations on the representation can change the concepts expressed by the generator. Examples using Stable Diffusion demonstrate this approach. The contribution connects a structural account of learned representations with a practical means of controlling generation through operations on those representations.
neurips-2023-concept-algebra-for-score-b.tldr: The paper formalizes concept subspaces in score-based generators and demonstrates concept control through algebraic representation edits.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy from an existing dataset. As the policy changes, it can favor behavior unlike the data, causing overly optimistic value estimates and potentially learning failure. Conservative approaches address this problem by penalizing estimates involving unfamiliar states or actions. This paper shifts the focus to estimating the value of states directly.

Conservative State Value Estimation, or CSVE, imposes penalties on states outside the data distribution to learn a conservative V-function. The authors present conservative guarantees and use the approach in an actor-critic algorithm. Its critic samples and penalizes states around the dataset, while its actor combines advantage-weighted updates with state exploration to improve the policy.

This construction connects cautious state evaluation with the policy update itself: the critic shapes which states appear valuable, and the actor uses those evaluations when learning behavior. On D4RL continuous-control tasks, the method outperforms the conservative Q-function learning methods evaluated and remains strongly competitive with recent leading approaches. These findings support state-value conservatism as a useful offline learning strategy.
neurips-2023-conservative-state-value-es.tldr: CSVE penalizes unfamiliar states to learn conservative state values and improve offline policy learning.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains artificial neural networks successfully, but its relationship to biological learning remains unresolved. One concern is the symmetry required between weights carrying signals forward and backward. This paper proposes a different organizing objective for supervised learning: maximize correlative information between the activities of network layers.

The authors combine this objective with mean squared error for fitting labeled examples and optimize it through coordinate descent. The resulting network resembles a more biologically realistic arrangement of pyramidal neurons with multiple compartments, dendritic processing, and lateral inhibitory neurons. The architecture arises from the proposed optimization framework, connecting the learning objective to the mechanisms used for signal propagation.

A central result uses two mathematically equivalent forms of the correlative information objective. These yield forward and backward prediction networks without the weight symmetry issue associated with conventional backpropagation. The work therefore supplies a proposed learning framework that addresses several biological plausibility concerns. Its contribution is a mechanistic alternative for modeling supervised learning, while whether the brain uses such learning remains an open question.
neurips-2023-correlative-information-max.tldr: Correlative information maximization yields a biologically motivated supervised network without requiring symmetric forward and backward weights.

paragraphs: Counting unique elements becomes difficult under person-level differential privacy when one person can contribute arbitrarily many items. Removing that person could change the count by an arbitrarily large amount. This means the original query has unbounded sensitivity, making the size of an individual's possible effect central to the privacy problem.

The paper replaces the original count with an approximation whose sensitivity is bounded. Computing this alternative query reduces to a maximum-flow problem, giving a concrete optimization procedure for obtaining the bounded-sensitivity answer. The approach therefore changes the quantity being computed before adding the noise needed to protect privacy.

Choosing the sensitivity bound creates a trade-off. A tighter bound limits how much privacy noise is needed, but can make the approximation less faithful to the actual number of unique elements. A looser bound moves the balance in the other direction. The authors optimize this bound to balance approximation error against privacy noise, directly addressing the difficulty created by unrestricted contributions from individual people.
neurips-2023-counting-distinct-elements-.tldr: A maximum-flow-based approximation balances privacy noise and counting error when individuals can contribute unlimited items.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks repeatedly combine information across nodes. With increasing depth, node representations can become so similar that meaningful distinctions disappear, a phenomenon called oversmoothing. Although this behavior was established for graph convolutional networks, whether attention could prevent it remained disputed. This paper addresses that question through mathematical analysis.

The authors treat attention-based graph networks as nonlinear dynamical systems whose behavior changes across layers. Their framework uses products of varying matrices and the joint spectral radius to analyze repeated aggregation. It accommodates operators that are asymmetric, depend on current node representations, and vary over time, along with several widely used nonlinear activation functions.

For the models covered by the analysis, attention does not prevent oversmoothing: expressive power decreases exponentially with depth. The framework broadens earlier results for symmetric graph convolutions to include random-walk convolutions, graph attention networks, and graph transformers. The result explains why adapting aggregation weights through attention does not by itself remove the loss of node distinctions caused by repeated aggregation.
neurips-2023-demystifying-oversmoothing-.tldr: The analysis shows that attention does not prevent exponential oversmoothing in the broad class of graph networks studied.

paragraphs: Sampling-based theories of brain function interpret neural activity as samples from probability distributions used in computation. A key mechanistic question is how neural dynamics could generate samples from complicated distributions. This paper investigates which recurrent network architectures have sufficient expressive capacity for that role.

The authors first examine traditional sampler-only networks, where neuron outputs directly serve as samples. They argue that standard synaptic-current and firing-rate dynamics in this arrangement have limited sampling capacity. They then show that adding a separate set of output units gives recurrent firing-rate circuits the capacity to sample from arbitrary probability distributions. They call this architecture a reservoir-sampler network.

To train these networks, the paper uses denoising score matching to find recurrent and output weights that implement Langevin sampling. Experiments demonstrate sampling from several complex data distributions. Together, the architectural result and training procedure provide a route from an abstract probabilistic account of neural computation to an explicit model of neural dynamics with substantially greater sampling expressiveness.
neurips-2023-expressive-probabilistic-sa.tldr: Separating recurrent dynamics from output units enables expressive neural samplers trained through denoising score matching.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning could make use of large collections of reward-free experience, but learning from offline data is difficult when goals are far away. Estimating the value of actions for distant goals can be inaccurate. HIQL uses the structure of goal reaching: a long journey passes through closer subgoals, whose immediate usefulness is typically easier to assess.

The method learns two policies from one action-free value function. A high-level policy selects a latent representation of a state to serve as a subgoal. A low-level policy chooses the action for reaching that subgoal. This hierarchy divides distant goal selection and nearby action selection into related learning problems.

Analysis and illustrative examples show how the decomposition makes the method robust to noise in value estimates. On offline goal-reaching benchmarks, HIQL solves long-horizon tasks that challenge prior methods, handles high-dimensional image observations, and uses action-free data. These findings support hierarchy as a way to make goal-directed learning more effective when value estimates for distant outcomes are unreliable.
neurips-2023-hiql-offline-goal-condition.tldr: HIQL learns subgoal and action policies from offline data to make long-horizon goal reaching more robust to noisy value estimates.

paragraphs: Truncated data arise when observations from part of a distribution's possible range are never seen. Estimating the original distribution then requires accounting for an entire missing region. This paper studies how to perform that extrapolation efficiently, extending earlier algorithmic results for Gaussian distributions and linear regression with Gaussian noise.

The authors develop an estimation algorithm for log-concave exponential families, a broader distribution class. Their method uses projected stochastic gradient descent. The stated result establishes polynomial sample and time complexity on average, showing that efficient estimation from truncated observations is possible beyond the previously studied Gaussian settings.

The paper also presents the algorithm as simpler and more efficient than recent alternatives. Its significance is the combination of a broader estimation setting and an accessible optimization procedure: the missing observations do not rule out efficient recovery throughout the distribution class considered. The work additionally identifies implications for learning general log-concave distributions and for sampling when the only available data have been truncated.
neurips-2023-learning-exponential-famili.tldr: Projected stochastic gradient descent enables efficient estimation of log-concave exponential families from truncated observations.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses among options while learning their rewards. This paper studies a difficult combination: rewards can be heavy-tailed, some observations follow Huber's contamination model, and the learner must preserve differential privacy. The analysis covers distributions with a finite kth raw moment or a finite kth central moment, for k at least two.

The authors first establish a minimax lower bound on regret, describing unavoidable losses as privacy requirements, contamination, and heavy tails vary. They then build a general algorithm around private, robust mean estimation. Its estimation routines use reward truncation and the Laplace mechanism, with separate constructions for the two moment settings.

The resulting bandit algorithms achieve nearly optimal regret. The proposed truncation-based and histogram-based mean estimators also attain optimal trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, and robustness. Experimental studies support the theoretical findings. The contribution links the fundamental difficulty of private, contaminated decision-making to concrete estimation procedures that approach those limits under the stated moment assumptions.
neurips-2023-on-private-and-robust-bandi.tldr: Private, robust reward estimators enable nearly optimal bandit regret under contamination and heavy-tailed rewards.

paragraphs: Kernelized bandit learning seeks the optimum of a function using noisy evaluations at sequentially chosen points. The function belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which specifies its structure. GP-UCB is a popular algorithm for this problem, but previous regret bounds were too weak to establish sublinear regret for several common kernels, including Matérn kernels.

This paper improves the analysis by regularizing kernel ridge estimators according to the smoothness of the kernel. It combines that idea with a concentration result for separable Hilbert spaces and supplies an independent, simplified derivation of that result. The key change is a tighter mathematical treatment of estimation uncertainty.

The resulting bounds show nearly optimal regret for GP-UCB and establish sublinear regret rates for Matérn kernels. Sublinear cumulative regret means that average regret per decision decreases as learning continues. These findings show that earlier bounds understated the algorithm's performance and partially resolve the cited open problem concerning its theoretical guarantees.
neurips-2023-on-the-sublinear-regret-of-.tldr: A tighter analysis establishes nearly optimal GP-UCB regret, including sublinear rates for Matérn kernels.

paragraphs: Personalized subject swapping aims to replace the subject in an existing image with a particular subject supplied through reference images. The challenge includes preserving the original image's composition and coherence while expressing the replacement subject's identity. Photoswap addresses this task using pretrained diffusion models and control over their attention mechanisms.

The procedure first learns a visual concept from reference images of the desired subject. It then performs the swapping stage without additional training, manipulating self-attention and cross-attention to transfer that concept into the target image. The paper connects successful transfer to having a well-formed subject concept and appropriately controlling attention, while maintaining pose and image coherence.

Experiments support the method's effectiveness and controllability. Human ratings favor Photoswap over the evaluated baselines for subject replacement, background preservation, and overall quality. These separate assessment dimensions matter because a convincing personalized edit must both depict the intended subject and retain the surrounding image. The findings support the method's usefulness for controlled editing of existing photographs.
neurips-2023-photoswap-personalized-subj.tldr: Photoswap learns a reference subject and uses diffusion attention control to insert it into existing images while preserving composition.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy information to guide the search for better solutions. This paper studies what becomes possible when an algorithm receives a quantum generalization of a stochastic gradient oracle. The access model is central: the results concern optimization with this quantum source of information about the function.

For Lipschitz convex functions, the authors introduce two methods with trade-offs between dimension and accuracy that they prove cannot be achieved classically. One method is also asymptotically optimal in low-dimensional settings. These results identify both an advantage from quantum access and a setting in which the proposed method reaches the best asymptotic performance.

The paper additionally develops quantum algorithms for finding critical points of smooth nonconvex functions at rates not known to be achievable classically. That statement differs in strength from the proven classical separation for the convex case. The methods build on quantum multivariate mean estimation and introduce a general quantum variance-reduction technique that supports the optimization results and is presented as independently useful.
neurips-2023-quantum-speedups-for-stocha.tldr: Quantum gradient access enables provable convex optimization speedups and new rates for finding nonconvex critical points.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making must balance collecting useful information with choosing actions that already appear rewarding. One way to study this balance is a saddle-point game: a learner chooses a sampling distribution while an adversary selects plausible models that could produce large regret. The decision-estimation coefficient, or DEC, provides nearly tight regret bounds through this perspective.

The authors reformulate the offset DEC in terms of a confidence radius and solve the resulting minimax problem. This produces Anytime-E2D, a variant of the Estimation-To-Decisions algorithm. Its central feature is that it optimizes the exploration-exploitation trade-off during learning, placing that decision inside the algorithm rather than leaving it to the theoretical analysis.

The formulation yields a practical algorithm for finite model classes and linear feedback models. The paper also relates the approach to the information ratio, decoupling coefficient, and PAC-DEC, and evaluates E2D numerically on simple examples. The contribution connects a theoretical characterization of decision difficulty with an operational method for adapting how the learner gathers information.
neurips-2023-regret-minimization-via-sad.tldr: Anytime-E2D uses saddle-point optimization to adjust the exploration-exploitation trade-off online.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents must make decisions under environmental uncertainty, changing behavior from other agents, and incomplete observations. When decisions also account for risk, coordinating independently acting agents becomes harder. This paper asks how each agent's risk-sensitive choices can agree with the risk-sensitive choice of a centralized policy.

The authors formalize that requirement through the Risk-sensitive Individual-Global-Max principle, or RIGM. It extends earlier coordination principles by requiring agreement under risk-sensitive action selection. Existing value-factorization methods do not satisfy this requirement for common measures such as Value at Risk and distorted risk measures. RiskQ addresses the mismatch by representing joint-return quantiles as weighted mixtures of quantiles from individual agents' return utilities.

The paper shows that RiskQ satisfies RIGM for Value at Risk and distorted risk metrics. This supplies a formal connection between decentralized choices and the central risk objective. Extensive experiments also show promising performance. The contribution combines a precise coordination criterion with a distributional representation designed to meet it, making risk sensitivity part of how cooperative value estimates are assembled.
neurips-2023-riskq-risk-sensitive-multi-.tldr: RiskQ factorizes return distributions so decentralized risk-sensitive choices agree with a centralized policy for specified risk metrics.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization searches for a good solution using function evaluations rather than gradients. This paper studies quadratic objectives and asks how their geometry determines the number of noisy evaluations needed. The Hessian describes that geometry, so the goal is a sample-complexity characterization that reflects the particular objective instead of treating all quadratics alike.

The authors introduce energy allocation to describe the interaction between the algorithm's search and the objective's geometry. This concept supports information-theoretic lower bounds on the required samples. Solving for an optimal energy spectrum gives a matching upper bound, yielding a tight characterization of the best Hessian-dependent sample complexity.

The paper then establishes the existence of an algorithm that does not require the Hessian as input yet attains the asymptotically optimal sample complexity for every Hessian instance. A truncation technique extends the stated optimal complexities to heavy-tailed noise distributions. The results connect geometry-specific limits with an algorithm capable of achieving those limits without being given the geometry in advance.
neurips-2023-sample-complexity-for-quadr.tldr: The paper tightly characterizes geometry-dependent quadratic optimization complexity and establishes an asymptotically optimal algorithm without Hessian input.

paragraphs: Class imbalance occurs when some categories have far more training examples than others, and it can hurt neural network performance. Much work addresses this through specialized loss functions or sampling rules. This paper investigates how far ordinary training components can go when they are tuned for the imbalanced setting.

The study considers batch size, data augmentation, network size, pretraining, optimizer choice, and label smoothing. The authors demonstrate that tuning these existing components can achieve state-of-the-art performance without specialized losses or samplers. The result highlights the importance of the overall training configuration when judging what is needed to learn effectively from unequal class frequencies.

The paper also offers training prescriptions and considerations, together with an account of why methods for imbalance succeed or fail. Its practical contribution is evidence that strong performance can come from configuring familiar pipeline elements appropriately. This supports treating those choices as a substantial part of the imbalance problem, while the stated result is that they can achieve leading performance, rather than that every imbalanced dataset needs the same configuration.
neurips-2023-simplifying-neural-network-.tldr: Tuning standard training components can achieve state-of-the-art performance under class imbalance without specialized losses or samplers.

paragraphs: An expressive neural network can behave like a much smaller model if neurons vanish or become redundant during training. This paper identifies a mechanism by which stochastic gradient descent encourages that simplification. It studies invariant sets in parameter space associated with sparse or low-rank subnetworks and asks when training dynamics are attracted toward them.

The analysis gives a sufficient condition for stochastic attraction based on the balance between local loss curvature and gradient noise. Increasing noise can strengthen attraction, even toward invariant sets associated with saddle points or local maxima of training loss. Thus, the noisy dynamics can favor simpler structures in ways that loss curvature alone would not suggest.

The authors observe attractive invariant sets in trained deep networks and demonstrate generalization benefits from stochastic collapse in a linear teacher-student setting. They also use the mechanism to explain why an extended early period with large learning rates can improve later generalization. The findings link gradient noise, reduced effective model complexity, and learning behavior through a specific dynamical account.
neurips-2023-stochastic-collapse-how-gra.tldr: Gradient noise can attract SGD toward simpler subnetworks, providing a mechanism for reduced complexity and improved generalization.

paragraphs: Interpretable graph neural networks identify the part of an input graph that influences a prediction. Existing approaches often depend on a particular dataset, making their explanations difficult to transfer. This paper introduces π-GNN to learn reusable structural patterns by pretraining on synthetic graphs with known explanations.

A structural pattern module extracts and combines diverse patterns to represent different graph types. A hypergraph refinement module then combines those patterns with local interactions among edges to identify the explanatory subgraph. For a downstream task, a task-specific predictor is connected to the pretrained model and the system is fine-tuned.

Experiments report improvements over leading interpretable graph network baselines of up to 9.98% in interpretation and 16.06% in classification accuracy. These are reported maxima, rather than gains claimed for every task. A model pretrained for graph classification also achieves top-tier interpretation performance on node classification. Together, the results support transferring explanation-related structural knowledge across downstream tasks while retaining a task-specific fine-tuning stage.
neurips-2023-train-once-and-explain-ever.tldr: π-GNN pretrains on synthetic graphs with known explanations to improve interpretability and transfer across graph tasks.

paragraphs: Fitting corrupted training labels does not always imply poor predictions on new examples. This paper studies that distinction for two-layer ReLU networks trained with gradient descent and hinge loss. The setting assumes linearly separable clean data with a relatively small proportion of labels flipped or corrupted.

The authors identify clean-data margin conditions producing three outcomes. In benign overfitting, training loss reaches zero while test classification is correct with high probability. In harmful overfitting, training loss also reaches zero, but test error has a constant lower bound. In non-overfitting, clean points reach zero loss while corrupted points do not, and test classification is again correct with high probability.

The proof follows neuron behavior through two training phases. Clean examples first approach zero loss; later, they oscillate near its boundary while corrupted examples either approach zero loss or are eventually zeroed by the network. By counting clean and corrupted updates, the analysis connects data geometry to whether fitting noisy labels helps, harms, or is avoided during training.
neurips-2023-training-shallow-relu-netwo.tldr: Margin conditions distinguish benign, harmful, and avoided overfitting in shallow ReLU networks trained on lightly corrupted labels.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning teaches a model to respond to requests using examples of instructions and answers. This paper extends machine-generated instruction training to language-and-image tasks. It uses language-only GPT-4 to produce multimodal instruction-following data, then trains a model intended for general visual and language understanding.

The resulting system, LLaVA, connects a vision encoder with a large language model and trains the combined model end to end. The researchers also construct two benchmarks containing diverse application-oriented tasks. These contributions provide both a training approach and evaluation resources for studying how models follow instructions involving images.

Experiments show multimodal conversation abilities, sometimes resembling multimodal GPT-4 behavior on unseen images and instructions. LLaVA receives an 85.1% relative score against GPT-4 on a synthetic instruction-following dataset. Separately, after Science QA fine-tuning, the combination of LLaVA and GPT-4 achieves 92.53% accuracy, reported as a new state of the art. The authors release the generated training data, model, and code to support further research.
neurips-2023-visual-instruction-tuning-4.tldr: LLaVA connects vision and language models through generated instruction data, demonstrating multimodal conversation and strong evaluated performance.

paragraphs: Indiscriminate data poisoning inserts crafted training examples to increase a model's overall test error. Some linear learners resist strong known attacks even without explicit defenses. This paper investigates whether that resistance can arise from the data distribution itself, rather than merely from an attack failing to find a damaging strategy.

For theoretical Gaussian distributions, the authors characterize an optimal poisoning attack: the strategy that maximizes the trained model's risk for a specified poisoning budget. Analyzing this strongest attack lets them study inherent robustness within the model. Their results show that robustness can occur when class distributions are well separated, have low variance, and the permitted poisoning points lie in a small constraint set.

These conditions connect attack effectiveness to both the geometry of clean data and the adversary's allowed inputs. The findings largely explain observed differences in the performance of leading poisoning attacks across benchmark datasets. The contribution is a conditional account of why some linear learning problems withstand poisoning better than others, grounded in an analysis of optimal attacks.
neurips-2023-what-distributions-are-robu.tldr: For Gaussian class distributions, separation, low variance, and restricted poisoning inputs can make linear learners inherently robust.

paragraphs: Generating a controllable human avatar involves more than positioning major body joints. Facial expression, jaw position, and hand pose are also important for expressive control. XAGen extends 3D human avatar generation to these attributes, addressing the limited attention earlier methods gave to fine-scale parts of the body.

The model uses a representation organized across multiple scales and body parts to capture small details in faces and hands. A corresponding rendering technique separates the synthesis of the body, face, and hands, with the aim of easing training and improving geometry. Multiple part-specific discriminators evaluate both visual appearance and the ability to express fine-grained controls.

These components jointly address detail and controllability: the representation models small regions, the renderer organizes their synthesis, and the discriminators assess the generated results. Experiments show XAGen surpassing the compared state-of-the-art methods in realism, diversity, and expressive control. The findings support treating face and hand generation as explicit parts of the avatar model when detailed human expression is a central objective.
neurips-2023-xagen-3d-expressive-human-a.tldr: XAGen uses multiscale, part-specific modeling and rendering to generate realistic 3D avatars with body, face, and hand control.
